before.overview: The original 1940 first-ascent line, climbed by teenage brothers Fred and Helmy Beckey on August 29, 1940 — one of the routes Beckey later named among his 100 favorite North American climbs. From a moat crossing at the toe of the ridge, about 1,300 vertical feet of sustained 5.6/5.7 climbing follows compact slab and corners low down; rock quality improves markedly higher on the ridge crest, finishing with ~200 ft of easy 5th-class scrambling and a short, featured summit headwall. This is also the standard descent line for parties finishing the East Ridge or South Face.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high; multi-day, trail-less approach with roughly 7,500 ft of elevation gain over brush, talus, and cross-country terrain to the Crescent Creek basin camp
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy overnight/glacier-travel kit (40-50+ lbs) for the multi-day approach plus a full alpine rock rack

partner_requirements.approachTime: 1-2 days of cross-country travel to reach the Crescent Creek basin camp before the climb itself
requiredSkills: Multi-pitch traditional rock leading at 5.7 with sustained exposure
Route-finding on an unmarked, trail-less approach and on the ridge itself
Glacier travel and crevasse rescue (standard kit for this zone per outside route beta)
Efficient rappelling/downclimbing on loose alpine rock for the descent
Self-sufficient multi-day wilderness travel and navigation in a remote, no-rescue-nearby setting
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Advanced to expert alpine climbers only - prior remote North Cascades/Pickets-style objectives strongly recommended before this one

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout off SR-20 behind a large boulder at Goodell Creek Campground; NPS wilderness permit required for overnight camping in the Terror/Crescent Creek basins.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground on SR-20, just west of Newhalem — an unmarked pullout behind a large boulder. If you plan to camp overnight in the Terror Creek or Crescent Creek basins, you'll need an NPS wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin climbers' path cairn
waypoints.note: Old roadbed ends and a rock cairn marks a hard right turnoff onto the steep, more-defined climbers' path, which runs atop a forested ridge here.
waypoints.directions: Walk the old streamside roadbed up the Goodell Creek valley at easy grades for about four miles, crossing the creek along the way. The last flowing water is near 1,600 ft and everything above is dry, so fill up there rather than counting on the basin. Watch the uphill side closely as you go: the turnoff is small, sometimes unmarked, and parties routinely stride past it and waste an hour on the valley trail.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin camp
waypoints.note: Glacial-outwash camping among streams below the Southern Pickets; treeline is passed around 5000-5200 ft on the way up.
waypoints.directions: The path goes straight up the forested hillside with no switchbacks and no let-up, a long haul on roots and dirt that most parties consider the hardest part of the whole approach. There is no water anywhere on it. Timber ends near 5,000-5,200 ft and the ground turns to meadow, slab and usually old snow, from where a rising traverse leads toward a broad saddle and the camping benches just below it.

waypoints.name: The Barrier crossing
waypoints.note: Loose, 'serious Class 3' rock rib separating Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin, just below Degenhardt; crossing higher avoids a longer traverse but involves a moat and low-5th-class moves — parties have turned back here.
waypoints.directions: Work up and across the basin toward Degenhardt to reach the rib. Where you cross it matters more than anything else on this leg — going in low is longer and brushier and has pulled parties onto fifth-class ground, while taking it high near the notch shortens the traverse but usually means dealing with a moat where the snow pulls back from the rock. The rock is loose enough throughout that a slip, not the technical grade, is the real hazard.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Established camp under Mount Terror used as the staging basin for Inspiration Peak's west side; this is the 'Crescent Creek basin camp' referenced in the route beta.
waypoints.directions: From the notch at the top of the rib, drop onto the snow ramp running down the far side, which is an easy descent while it still holds snow and turns into loose talus and open moats as the season goes on. It puts you straight into the basin under Terror at around 6,200 ft.

waypoints.name: West Ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave the basin talus/snow and scramble onto the crest of Inspiration's west ridge above camp.
waypoints.directions: Climb the talus and snow out of the basin and cross the glacier below the peak; it is crevassed, and the moat or bergschrund at its head is the usual obstacle in getting onto rock at all. Start up the obvious gully above it and follow that until stepping out onto the crest makes sense, roughly 300 ft above the ice.

waypoints.name: Exposed gneiss ridge steps
waypoints.note: Sequence of exposed 5.7 steps on loose gneiss along the ridge crest below the summit block — the technical crux of the route.
waypoints.directions: The first pitches are the poorest rock on the route: slabby compact ground where anchors are awkward to arrange, a large corner and chimney stacked with loose blocks, and lichen-covered ledge systems leading back toward the crest. Quality improves steadily with every pitch gained. Belay somewhere out of the fall line of what the leader is going to pull off.

waypoints.name: Inspiration Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Inspiration Peak in the Southern Pickets; descend by rappelling the west ridge crest with a single 60m rope back to the glacier above the moat.
waypoints.directions: Once the crest proper is underfoot the rock turns solid and well featured, and easy fifth class runs a couple of hundred feet to the base of the summit headwall. The last pitches take the headwall itself on good holds, passing a pale rock scar on the way to the top.

itinerary.cal: Goodell Creek approach is typically dry and climbable July-September; earlier in the season expect more snow on the steep 3,600 ft forested slope and the Terror Glacier crossing.

days.note: From the Goodell Creek trailhead, hike ~4 mi of brushy trail along the creek, then grind up an unrelenting, viewless ~3,600 ft of steep forested slope with no switchbacks, finishing with a rising traverse to a ~6,200 ft saddle and a short descent into Terror Basin. Real trip reports clock this leg at roughly 6.5 hours.
days.title: Approach to Terror Basin

days.note: A long alpine day: cross the Terror Glacier (crampons on, watch for the mid-glacier icefall), gain the base of the ridge, then climb ~14 pitches of low-5th-class rock to the summit. Descend the same ridge crest by rappel/downclimb combo back to the glacier and camp.

days.note: Reverse the approach: scree/scramble up out of the basin, over the saddle, and down the steep forested slope back to the creek trail. Most parties take it easier than the way in but still budget most of a day given the terrain.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the bergschrund at the toe of the ridge and climb an approach gully until it makes sense to break out onto the ridge proper; loose, glacier-polished rock near the schrund.

Continue up compact slab low on the ridge to gain the crest; protection is sparse on this low-angle friction, and a 3-pin anchor here was rebuilt in June 2024 because natural gear placements are scarce.
Face climbing just right of the ridge crest on sustained, compact slab — the start of roughly 1,300 vertical feet of sustained 5.6/5.7 climbing that defines the lower route.
Continued sustained slab climbing on the lower ridge; holds are small and rounded, rewarding careful footwork over strength.
Slab and low-angle corners lead to a 2-pin anchor below a left-facing corner; rock quality is noticeably better here than down at the schrund.
Climb the left-facing corner directly; clean edges and a steady crack make this one of the better-protected pitches on the lower ridge.
Head up and right via a series of corners to a sloping ledge with a 2-pin anchor; sustained, technical corner climbing.

A large, obvious corner capped by a short chimney; awkward stemming and a step left onto slab make this the technical crux of the West Ridge, even though it's graded the same as several pitches below.
Slab climbing directly above the chimney corner, easing off slightly as the ridge crest broadens.
A rising, exposed traverse of about 100 feet across lichen-covered ledges to a small horn slung with cord for the belay; route-finding along the ledge system matters more than raw difficulty.
Climb back onto the ridge crest on markedly better rock than lower down — clean, solid granite typical of the upper mountain.
Roughly 200 feet of easy 5th-class scrambling along the crest to the base of the summit headwall; still roped given the exposure on both sides of the narrow ridge.
Climb the right side of the short, featured summit headwall to a horn-and-pin anchor; solid rock with good edges on a steep, exposed final move.
Pull through a rock-scar roof low on the pitch, then run out about 200 feet of lower-angle rock to the summit ridge — the last pitch of the climb, topping out just short of the true summit.

approach_variants.name: Goodell Creek and the stone-arrow boot path to Terror Basin, then the crevassed Terror Glacier to the bergschrund below the west end of the peak
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead and group campground just west of Newhalem off SR-20 and pick up the Goodell Creek Trail. The first roughly 4 miles follow an old streamside roadbed at easy grades from about 500 to 1,600 ft, crossing the creek and passing the LAST RELIABLE FLOWING WATER AROUND 1,600 FT. Fill up there; the trail is dry above.

A cairned stone-arrow junction, sometimes marked and sometimes not, sends climbers off the valley trail onto a steep, switchback-free boot path that claws straight up the forested hillside, gaining roughly 3,400-4,000 ft in about a mile and a half of unrelenting root-and-dirt tree climbing with no water and no easy grades. Parties widely describe this as the crux of the whole approach.

The boot path breaks out of timber around 5,000-5,200 ft into meadows, slabs and often snow, and a rising traverse north-northeast leads to a broad saddle at roughly 6,000-6,200 ft. Camp is typically just below it in Terror Creek Basin.
hazards: A heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing below the peak's south side; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
A bergschrund and a moat at the base that open through the season
Compact rock with scarce placements on the lower pitches
Loose blocks on the lower ledges
No water for the last 3,500 ft of the climb to camp
A rappel descent of 12-14 stations, with traversing raps that are rockfall-prone and stations that are hard to spot
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT A BERGSCHRUND AND CLIMBS 300 FT OF GULLY TO THE TOE OF THE RIDGE, AND THAT IS AN EXACT INSTRUCTION. From camp, cross heather and snow slopes trending north-northwest, losing a little elevation to cross the outlet drainage from a small tarn just southeast of the McMillan Spires, then regain ground on slabs and snow up to the edge of the Terror Glacier. LEAVE THE GLACIER AT THE BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END OF THE PEAK and climb roughly 300 FT OF GULLY to reach the toe of the west ridge, where the roped climbing begins.

SO THE SCHRUND IS THE MARKER AND THE 300 FT IS THE MEASURE. The schrund and the moat where snow meets rock are the variable part; they open through the season and the crossing is easiest with continuous snow early. A party that has climbed a short gully and reached the toe of a ridge is at the base; a party still on ice has not started.

THE DISCRIMINATOR AGAINST THE SOUTH FACE, WHICH STARTS OFF THE SAME GLACIER AND IS THE COMMONEST CONFUSION HERE: the SOUTH FACE starts at the LOWER-LEFT CORNER of the south face WHERE A SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS MEETS THE GLACIER. This route starts at the WEST END of the peak, at a schrund, and goes UP A GULLY FIRST. If you are roping up at a buttress toe that touches the ice directly, with no gully above you, you are on the South Face.

CONFIRM ON THE CLIMB: the first pitches work through corner systems and LICHEN-COVERED LEDGES on compact rock where placements are scarce. Above them the line gains the crest itself and the rock quality improves steadily, described as extremely good on the crest. Total climbing above the schrund is about 1,300 ft in 14 pitches. If the rock is good from the first pitch, you are not on the lower corners of this route.

A HOUSEKEEPING RULE FROM THE ROUTE'S OWN PRACTICE: loose blocks sit on the lower ledges and the standard practice is to clear them deliberately once the second is out of the fall line rather than leave them for a following party.

Reserve on Recreation.gov — early-access lottery runs Mar 24-Apr 21 for the May 15-Oct 10 peak season, with general on-sale April 29; ~40% of inventory is held for walk-up permits at the Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount.

before.descent_text: The standard descent from the summit goes down the West Ridge crest itself, then finishes down Inspiration's South Face — it is not a walk-off. Most recent parties (e.g. a well-documented July 2024 ascent) report roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge on a single 60-70m rope, using a mix of fixed slings/rap rings left by prior parties (quality varies — some stations have been found tattered and worth backing up or replacing) and natural nut/cam anchors built on the spot. After the ridge raps, parties briefly stow the rope and downclimb/scramble 3rd-4th class terrain to a notch, from which roughly 9 more single-rope rappels descend the South Face to the Terror Glacier, for a total in the neighborhood of 12-14 rappels overall — the final rappel often runs nearly the full 60-70m to reach flat glacier snow. Some parties instead descend the full length of the West Ridge on a doubled/twin-rope system, using longer double-rope rappels off natural gear (solid nut placements) to cut the total rappel count to around 7, bypassing the separate South Face section — either line is used depending on party preference and rope setup. Watch for loose, rockfall-prone rock on the traversing stations (some raps go sideways, not straight down, to reach the next anchor and to dodge fall lines), stay alert for hard-to-spot anchor stations, and re-rope for glacier travel the instant you're back on the Terror Glacier at the bottom. From the glacier, reverse the approach: back across the crevassed glacier and slabs to Terror Basin camp, then down the steep boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead — parties frequently finish this exit in the dark, with some trip reports noting arrival at camp or the car well after nightfall.

before.rappels: 5-8 rappels down the West Ridge (some parties add rappels down the South Face gully); 70m rope recommended for fewer, longer raps; some anchors reported with thin/worn tat — carry extra cord.

days.note: Same brutal approach shared by all Inspiration Peak routes: brushy Goodell Creek trail, then a steep ~3,600+ ft forested slog with no switchbacks up to a saddle and down into Terror Basin camp.

days.note: An all-day alpine outing: scramble and glacier-travel to the route start, then climb 4 pitches of 5.7 to gain the ridge crest followed by 4 more moderate pitches to the summit (~8 hrs of climbing). There is no walk-off — the descent is 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge, a scramble to a notch, then 9 more rappels (some with traverses) down the South Face back to the glacier.

before.approach: This route shares the Goodell Creek trailhead and the same long approach as the West Ridge/South Face routes: the Goodell Creek Trail runs ~4 easy miles along the creek from the trailhead (near the group campground west of Newhalem, off SR-20) to about 1,600 ft, where the last reliable water is found, then a steep, switchback-free climbers' boot path grinds up roughly 3,400-4,000 ft of forested hillside with no water to reach timberline around 5,000-5,200 ft. Above timberline, a rising traverse on meadow, slab, and snow leads to the broad saddle at ~6,000-6,200 ft, with camp typically made just below it in Terror Creek Basin. From camp, the route to the base of the East Ridge continues across glacier-scoured slabs and onto the Terror Glacier beneath Inspiration's South Face — the glacier crossing is low-angle but heavily crevassed, generally with adequate snow bridges in season, so rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear. Unlike the West Ridge and South Face lines, the East Ridge start is reached by continuing around/across the glacier below the South Face and gaining a col that puts you at the true start of the East Ridge proper; from there the ridge climbing begins immediately with sustained exposure. Total approach is roughly 7 miles and 6,000+ ft of gain from the trailhead to the base of the route, typically consuming most of a full day, and this is consistently rated one of the longer, more strenuous approaches in the North Cascades — budget an early alpine start on summit day given the distance already covered just to reach camp.

approach_variants.name: As for the West Ridge and South Face to the Terror Glacier, then around and across the glacier BELOW the South Face to the col at the east end
approach_variants.notes:
Shares the Goodell Creek trailhead and the same long approach as the West Ridge and South Face: about 4 easy miles along the creek to roughly 1,600 ft and the last reliable water, then a steep switchback-free climbers' boot path grinding up 3,400-4,000 ft of forested hillside with no water to timberline around 5,000-5,200 ft, then a rising traverse on meadow, slab and snow to the broad saddle at 6,000-6,200 ft with camp just below it in Terror Creek Basin.

From camp the ground to the base runs across glacier-scoured slabs and onto the Terror Glacier beneath Inspiration's South Face. This is consistently rated one of the longer, more strenuous approaches in the North Cascades, and reaching the base alone typically consumes most of a full day.
hazards: A low-angle but heavily crevassed Terror Glacier crossing; rope up and carry crevasse-rescue gear
Sustained exposure from the first moves off the col
Poorer, looser rock than the peak's other lines
No established descent; the way down is 12-14 rappels on other routes' ground
An approach that consumes most of a full day before the climb starts
Parties commonly finish the exit after dark
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ROUTE YOU REACH BY KEEPING GOING, AND THE NEGATIVE TEST IS THE STRONGEST THING ABOUT IT. Unlike the West Ridge and South Face lines, the East Ridge start is reached by CONTINUING AROUND AND ACROSS THE GLACIER BELOW THE SOUTH FACE and gaining a col at the far end that puts you at the true start of the ridge.

SO, IN ORDER, WHAT YOU PASS AND MUST NOT STOP AT: first the BERGSCHRUND BELOW THE WEST END with a 300 ft gully above it, which is the West Ridge. Then the SMALL ROCK BUTTRESS AT THE LOWER-LEFT CORNER OF THE SOUTH FACE where rock meets ice, which is the South Face. If you have roped up at either, you have stopped one or two routes short of this one. Keep walking east until the face ends and the ground rises to a gap.

ARRIVAL: a col at the east end of the peak. From there the ridge climbing begins IMMEDIATELY with sustained exposure, which is itself the confirmation. There is no walk-in above this col and no easing-off; if the ground above you is scrambling terrain, you are not on the East Ridge.

WHAT IS NOT KNOWN: nothing published names the col or gives it a height, and this is a Grade IV 5.9 with very light traffic. What is recorded is its POSITION IN A SEQUENCE, which is why the base finding is written as a sequence rather than as a feature.

AND THE FACT THAT SHOULD BE READ BEFORE STARTING, NOT AFTER: there is NO established East Ridge descent. The way down combines the upper West Ridge and the South Face, the same descent West Ridge climbers use, because the East Ridge is reported as distinctly poorer, looser rock for descending and nobody downclimbs it. So you will have to find the other two routes' ground anyway, in the dark, tired, from above.

before.overview: Widely regarded as one of the best rock routes in the Picket Range and among Fred Beckey's favorite North American climbs. First climbed by Fred Beckey, Dave Collins, and Ed Cooper in October 1958 (weekend of Oct 5), on a second attempt at the then-unclimbed east ridge. The route starts at the base of the south face, gains a col to reach the ridge proper, then follows about 8-10 pitches of mid-5th to 5.9 climbing on sustained, exposed, excellent rock, highlighted by a 30m sustained 5.9 hand-and-fist crack and an airy final low-5th traverse across the summit ridge to the top.

before.overview: The most direct line up Inspiration Peak: about 600 ft (4 pitches) of clean rock, reached by crossing the glacier to a small buttress under the south face. Climb up and right to a right-trending ramp, belay below a corner system, then trend up and left to connect with the obvious 'Great Gash' — a chimney splitting the upper south face — and chimney to the top. First ascent party/date not known.

partner_requirements.fitnessSpec: 12-hour round trip from high camp for the 1970 first-ascent party, atop a multi-day remote approach
partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day approach into the Southern Pickets via the Terror Glacier
requiredSkills: Roped glacier travel and crevasse rescue (Terror Glacier crossing)
Solid 5.8 trad leading with chimney/inside-corner technique — crux is the ~400 ft 'Great Gash' (5.8)
Routefinding through a branching ramp system
Self-rescue mindset given the Picket Range's remoteness
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Advanced — roped glacier travel plus sustained 5.8 alpine trad leading

before.descent_text: Standard descent is down the West Ridge, not back down the South Face. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a few hundred feet toward a notch on the ridge, then begin rappelling. Multiple trip reports of this exact route confirm it as a sustained multi-rappel descent through a gully/notch system with no fixed or bolted stations anywhere on the peak — every anchor is built from gear (nuts, small-to-medium cams, occasionally a slung horn), so carry a rack sufficient for both the climb and for leaving/building rappel anchors, plus some cord or rap tat. One detailed trip report of this route logged 7 double-rope rappels down the West Ridge line back to the Terror Glacier, building a fresh natural anchor at each station; a separate party descending the same general line but counting differently (single 70m rope, more, shorter pitches) reported roughly 5 rappels down the upper West Ridge to a notch followed by about 9 more rappels down through the gully/South Face terrain to the glacier, with several rappels traversing hard to one side to reach the next station and the final rappel using nearly the full rope length to reach a flat spot on the ice. Bring two ropes. The stations recorded on this line sit roughly 60 m apart, and a single 70 m rope doubled reaches only about 35 m — it does not reach them, so on one rope expect to build roughly twice as many anchors: about 14 rappels of 30-35 m, which is what the single-rope party above ended up doing. Expect loose rock in the gully and real risk of the rope hanging up on the traversing raps, so back up rappels and check pulls carefully. The descent ends back on the Terror Glacier at the base of the West Ridge/South Face, from which you re-cross the icefall (same crevasse hazard as the approach, now on tired legs and possibly softer afternoon snow) to regain camp, then reverse the Terror Basin boot path and Goodell Creek Trail to the trailhead.

rappel_detail.pull: Loose blocks sit on this line; clear what you safely can rather than pulling ropes down onto it.
rappel_detail.notes: First rappel off the West Ridge below the notch; no fixed anchors anywhere on this peak, station built fresh from gear.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/small-med cams, occasional slung horn)
hazards: accounts differ on how much fixed material is in place - some describe stations roughly a rope length apart on fixed pins, nuts and cord, reported replaced in mid-2024, while others describe building every anchor from gear. Carry cord and a rack for anchors either way.
rappel_detail.station: The descent is the West Ridge, not the South Face. The stations are on the skier's-left / west side of the summit; descend the ridge crest from there toward the base of the headwall.

rappel_detail.notes: Continuing down the West Ridge rappel line toward the Terror Glacier.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/cams/slung horn)
rappel_detail.station: A large horn anchor, reached by scrambling down the ridge crest.

rappel_detail.notes: Natural anchor built fresh at this station, as at every station on this descent.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/cams/slung horn)
hazards: free-hanging off the overhang, with the next station offset rather than straight below
rappel_detail.station: A three-pin anchor at the start of the ridge; the rappel from it goes down and climber's right off a large overhang.

rappel_detail.notes: Mid-line rappel down steep West Ridge terrain.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/cams/slung horn)
rappel_detail.station: Around here the line reaches the notch of the West Ridge gully and switches onto the South Face - one party counted about three and a half double-rope rappels down the ridge to just above that notch, then four more down the face.

rappel_detail.notes: Continuing the descent; two ropes used doubled/joined for close to full-length rappels.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/cams/slung horn)

rappel_detail.notes: Second-to-last rappel before reaching glacier-adjacent terrain.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/cams/slung horn)

rappel_detail.notes: Final rappel reaching the Terror Glacier; unrope and walk off from here.
rappel_detail.anchor: gear anchor (nuts/cams/slung horn)
hazards: bergschrund immediately below the landing
rockfall onto the base of the route, which is where stashed packs sit
rappel_detail.station: The final rappel is short - about 100 ft by one party's estimate - off a slab anchor of two pins and a nut, landing back on the Terror Glacier above the bergschrund. On the South Face variant it returns you to the base of the route itself, so gear can be left there.

access.fees: $10 per person plus a $6 non-refundable reservation fee for an overnight backcountry permit; youth 15 and under free. The fee season runs mid-May to early October.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (which includes most Picket Range approaches; 12 in on-trail corridors). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.
